17: Introduction
18: ============
19: 
20: What is pycparser?
21: ------------------
22: 
23: **pycparser** is a parser for the C language, written in pure Python. It is a
24: module designed to be easily integrated into applications that need to parse
25: C source code.
26: 
27: What is it good for?
28: --------------------
29: 
30: Anything that needs C code to be parsed. The following are some uses for
31: **pycparser**, taken from real user reports:
32: 
33: * C code obfuscator
34: * Front-end for various specialized C compilers
35: * Static code checker
36: * Automatic unit-test discovery
37: * Adding specialized extensions to the C language
38: 
39: One of the most popular uses of **pycparser** is in the `cffi
40: <https://cffi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_ library, which uses it to parse the
41: declarations of C functions and types in order to auto-generate FFIs.
42: 
43: **pycparser** is unique in the sense that it's written in pure Python - a very
44: high level language that's easy to experiment with and tweak. To people familiar
45: with Lex and Yacc, **pycparser**'s code will be simple to understand. It also
46: has no external dependencies (except for a Python interpreter), making it very
47: simple to install and deploy.
48: 
49: Which version of C does pycparser support?
50: ------------------------------------------
51: 
52: **pycparser** aims to support the full C99 language (according to the standard
53: ISO/IEC 9899). Some features from C11 are also supported, and patches to support
54: more are welcome.
55: 
56: **pycparser** supports very few GCC extensions, but it's fairly easy to set
57: things up so that it parses code with a lot of GCC-isms successfully. See the
58: `FAQ <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/wiki/FAQ>`_ for more details.
59: 
60: What grammar does pycparser follow?
61: -----------------------------------
62: 
63: **pycparser** very closely follows the C grammar provided in Annex A of the C99
64: standard (ISO/IEC 9899).
65: 
66: How is pycparser licensed?
67: --------------------------
68: 
69: `BSD license <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/blob/main/LICENSE>`_.
70: 
71: Contact details
72: ---------------
73: 
74: For reporting problems with **pycparser** or submitting feature requests, please
75: open an `issue <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/issues>`_, or submit a
76: pull request.
77: 
78: 
79: Installing
80: ==========
81: 
82: Prerequisites
83: -------------
84: 
85: **pycparser** is being tested with modern versions of Python on
86: Linux, macOS and Windows. See `the CI dashboard <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/actions/workflows/ci.yml>`__
87: for details.
88: 
89: **pycparser** has no external dependencies.
90: 
91: Installation process
92: --------------------
93: 
94: The recommended way to install **pycparser** is with ``pip``::
95: 
96:     > pip install pycparser
97: 
98: Using
99: =====
100: 
101: Interaction with the C preprocessor
102: -----------------------------------
103: 
104: In order to be compilable, C code must be preprocessed by the C preprocessor -
105: ``cpp``. A compatible ``cpp`` handles preprocessing directives like ``#include`` and
106: ``#define``, removes comments, and performs other minor tasks that prepare the C
107: code for compilation.
108: 
109: For all but the most trivial snippets of C code **pycparser**, like a C
110: compiler, must receive preprocessed C code in order to function correctly. If
111: you import the top-level ``parse_file`` function from the **pycparser** package,
112: it will interact with ``cpp`` for you, as long as it's in your PATH, or you
113: provide a path to it.
114: 
115: Note also that you can use ``gcc -E`` or ``clang -E`` instead of ``cpp``. See
116: the ``using_gcc_E_libc.py`` example for more details. Windows users can download
117: and install a binary build of Clang for Windows `from this website
118: <http://llvm.org/releases/download.html>`_.
119: 
120: What about the standard C library headers?
121: ------------------------------------------
122: 
123: C code almost always ``#include``\s various header files from the standard C
124: library, like ``stdio.h``. While (with some effort) **pycparser** can be made to
125: parse the standard headers from any C compiler, it's much simpler to use the
126: provided "fake" standard includes for C11 in ``utils/fake_libc_include``. These
127: are standard C header files that contain only the bare necessities to allow
128: valid parsing of the files that use them. As a bonus, since they're minimal, it
129: can significantly improve the performance of parsing large C files.
130: 
131: The key point to understand here is that **pycparser** doesn't really care about
132: the semantics of types. It only needs to know whether some token encountered in
133: the source is a previously defined type. This is essential in order to be able
134: to parse C correctly.
135: 
136: See `this blog post
137: <https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2015/on-parsing-c-type-declarations-and-fake-headers>`_
138: for more details.
139: 
140: Note that the fake headers are not included in the ``pip`` package nor installed
141: via the package build (`#224 <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/issues/224>`_).
142: 
143: Basic usage
144: -----------
145: 
146: Take a look at the |examples|_ directory of the distribution for a few examples
147: of using **pycparser**. These should be enough to get you started. Please note
148: that most realistic C code samples would require running the C preprocessor
149: before passing the code to **pycparser**; see the previous sections for more
150: details.
151: 
152: .. |examples| replace:: ``examples``
153: .. _examples: examples
154: 
155: 
156: Advanced usage
157: --------------
158: 
159: The public interface of **pycparser** is well documented with comments in
160: ``pycparser/c_parser.py``. For a detailed overview of the various AST nodes
161: created by the parser, see ``pycparser/_c_ast.cfg``.
162: 
163: There's also a `FAQ available here <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/wiki/FAQ>`_.
164: In any case, you can always drop me an `email <eliben@gmail.com>`_ for help.
165: 
166: 
167: Modifying
168: =========
169: 
170: There are a few points to keep in mind when modifying **pycparser**:
171: 
172: * The code for **pycparser**'s AST nodes is automatically generated from a
173:   configuration file - ``_c_ast.cfg``, by ``_ast_gen.py``. If you modify the AST
174:   configuration, make sure to re-generate the code. This can be done by running
175:   the ``_ast_gen.py`` script (from the repository root or the
176:   ``pycparser`` directory).
177: * Read the docstring in the constructor of the ``CParser`` class for details
178:   on configuration and compatibility arguments.

203:   The **pycparser** module source code.

Introduction
============

What is pycparser?
------------------

**pycparser** is a parser for the C language, written in pure Python. It is a
module designed to be easily integrated into applications that need to parse
C source code.

What is it good for?
--------------------

Anything that needs C code to be parsed. The following are some uses for
**pycparser**, taken from real user reports:

* C code obfuscator
* Front-end for various specialized C compilers
* Static code checker
* Automatic unit-test discovery
* Adding specialized extensions to the C language

One of the most popular uses of **pycparser** is in the `cffi
<https://cffi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/>`_ library, which uses it to parse the
declarations of C functions and types in order to auto-generate FFIs.

**pycparser** is unique in the sense that it's written in pure Python - a very
high level language that's easy to experiment with and tweak. To people familiar
with Lex and Yacc, **pycparser**'s code will be simple to understand. It also
has no external dependencies (except for a Python interpreter), making it very
simple to install and deploy.

Which version of C does pycparser support?
------------------------------------------

**pycparser** aims to support the full C99 language (according to the standard
ISO/IEC 9899). Some features from C11 are also supported, and patches to support
more are welcome.

**pycparser** supports very few GCC extensions, but it's fairly easy to set
things up so that it parses code with a lot of GCC-isms successfully. See the
`FAQ <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/wiki/FAQ>`_ for more details.

What grammar does pycparser follow?
-----------------------------------

**pycparser** very closely follows the C grammar provided in Annex A of the C99
standard (ISO/IEC 9899).

How is pycparser licensed?

`BSD license <https://github.com/eliben/pycparser/blob/main/LICENSE>`_.

-----------------------------------

In order to be compilable, C code must be preprocessed by the C preprocessor -

341:     def _handle_pppragma(self) -> List[Token]:
342:         # Parse a full #pragma line; returns a list of tokens with 1 or 2
343:         # tokens - PPPRAGMA and an optional PPPRAGMASTR. If an empty list is
344:         # returned, it means an error occurred, or we're at the end of input.
345:         #
346:         # Examples:
347:         # - "#pragma" -> PPPRAGMA only
348:         # - "#pragma once" -> PPPRAGMA, PPPRAGMASTR("once")
349:         # - "# pragma omp parallel private(th_id)" -> PPPRAGMA, PPPRAGMASTR("omp parallel private(th_id)")
350:         # - "#\tpragma {pack: 2, smack: 3}" -> PPPRAGMA, PPPRAGMASTR("{pack: 2, smack: 3}")
351:         text = self._lexdata
352:         n = len(text)
353:         pos = self._pos
354: 
355:         while pos < n and text[pos] in " \t":
356:             pos += 1
357:         if pos >= n:
358:             self._pos = pos
359:             return []
360: 
361:         if not text.startswith("pragma", pos):
362:             self._error("invalid #pragma directive", pos)
363:             self._pos = pos + 1
364:             return []
365: 
366:         pragma_pos = pos
367:         pos += len("pragma")
368:         toks = [self._make_token("PPPRAGMA", "pragma", pragma_pos)]
369: 
370:         while pos < n and text[pos] in " \t":
371:             pos += 1
372: 
373:         start = pos
374:         while pos < n and text[pos] != "\n":
375:             pos += 1
376:         if pos > start:
377:             toks.append(self._make_token("PPPRAGMASTR", text[start:pos], start))
378:         if pos < n and text[pos] == "\n":
379:             self._lineno += 1
380:             pos += 1
381:             self._line_start = pos
382:         self._pos = pos
383:         return toks
